1:
The quarrel breaks out the moment the common enemy is down. Henry marks the timing: no sooner were the Midianites subdued than Israel was ready to fall out with itself, and the spark, had Gideon not put it out at once with a great deal of wisdom and grace, might have flamed into something fatal. Gill notes the occasion they chose — they came bringing the heads of Oreb and Zeeb, and took the delivery of them for the proper moment to chide. Ellicott traces the arrogance to its sources: the tribe's strength, the memory of Joseph, the double portion given him, Jacob's preferring the younger Ephraim before Manasseh in the blessing, and the almost regal influence long exercised by their tribesman Joshua. What they wanted was the acknowledgment of their claims by all the tribes — their hegemony, as the Greeks would have called it — and the same temper was to bring on them a terrible humiliation later. The words rendered they did chide with him sharply mean literally with force or violence, which the Vulgate turns as strongly reproaching him and almost offering him violence.

Henry takes the accusation apart. Gideon was called of God and acted as God directed, neither taking honour to himself nor disposing of honours, so that in quarrelling with him the Ephraimites were reflecting on the divine conduct. Then why did they not offer themselves? The enemy was in their own country and the forces raising against him were known; the case itself called them, and they needed no invitation. And he had in fact saved their credit by not calling them, since had they come, many would have gone back with the faint-hearted or been dismissed with the slothful. Cowards will seem valiant when the danger is over, Henry says, but those consult their reputation who do not try their courage when danger is near; and those most backward to difficult service are the readiest to censure a more enterprising spirit, and the angriest not to have the credit of it. Clarke raises a different objection, that the paragraph stands out of its place, since Gideon had not yet passed Jordan, and it was beyond the river that the heads were brought to him.

The answer itself is what everyone admires. Gideon set the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim above the vintage of Abiezer, and Clarke reads it as sober fact: they had taken the two Midianite generals, having discomfited their hosts at the passes of Jordan, and so had done the more important service. Ellicott finds the self-control noble precisely because Gideon was by no means a placable man; he was not in a condition to humble this kindred tribe as the more independent Jephthah afterwards did, and he remembered that Zebah and Zalmunna were still at large, so that patriotism as much as right feeling forbade civil discord at such a moment. The saying has a proverbial ring, and the Chaldee turns it, Are not the weak of the house of Ephraim better than the strong of the house of Abiezer? Henry observes that while Gideon was willing to diminish his own performance in order to magnify theirs, he would take no flowers from God's crown to adorn theirs. Clarke notes what he might have said and did not, that twenty-two thousand had once left him through faint-heartedness. Their anger was abated; Henry thinks some resentment remained, and that Gideon prudently let it cool by degrees.
4:
Ellicott takes the crossing to resume the narrative broken off in the previous chapter, the intervening verses being an episode brought in by anticipation to close the notice about Ephraim. Henry admires the firmness of it: he took none with him but his three hundred, who had now laid aside their trumpets and torches for swords and spears, confiding in the promise that by these three hundred God would save Israel. The phrase faint yet pursuing is disputed. Clarke reports the Vulgate's paraphrase, that through fatigue they could not overtake the fugitives; Ellicott doubts the usual application of the words and gives the Greek as fainting and hungry, following Keil and Delitzsch, who make the conjunction explanatory — exhausted, that is, with pursuing — and dismiss the Greek rendering as arbitrary and of no critical worth. Henry turns the phrase inward: fainting and yet pursuing is many a time the true Christian's case.

Succoth got its name from the booths Jacob raised there, as Gill and Ellicott both note, and lay east of Jordan in the tribe of Gad. Ellicott stresses how modest the request was — Gideon did not requisition forces or intelligence or any active help, since those east of Jordan would be the first to feel Midian's vengeance if the victory proved incomplete; to give bread to hungry countrymen was an act of common humanity the Midianites could hardly resent. Clarke says simply that a man engaged in the common cause of Israel had a right to expect succour, and that the request was just and reasonable. The refusal, Keil and Delitzsch argue, was not only cowardice — fear of what Midian might do to those who had supplied Gideon — but contempt for the small force he had. Ellicott says we cannot tell whether the tone was derision or mere fear, but that on any reading they were guilty of inhumanity, want of faith, want of courage and want of patriotism, and notes that they magnify the sacrifice by calling his followers an army, a word Gideon had not used. Clarke's verdict is that they dared not trust God. Henry's is blunter: the princes neither feared God nor regarded man, and shut up their compassion against their brethren — were these princes, were these Israelites?

The threat is severe and the commentators do not soften it. Keil and Delitzsch render it thresh rather than tear, a verb used figuratively for punishing severely, with desert thorns because the desert is the natural soil of thorn-bushes; and they reject the suggestion that the rare second word means threshing sledges set with flints. Ellicott prefers thresh on the same grounds and thinks it implies that the men were laid down and harrows driven over them after thorns had been scattered, noting that David appears to have done the like, and that here the horror was greater because the sufferers were Israelites and not aliens. He states the difficulty plainly: the verse mixes heroic faith with barbarous severity, and while the faith ennobled Gideon and made him an example, the ruthlessness belongs to the wild age he lived in and is no more to be approved than his later degeneracy. Henry explains the delay — Gideon would not lose time from the pursuit, nor seem to act in a heat of passion, and the reckoning would shame them more once he had done what they thought impracticable; meanwhile the warning left them space to repent. At Penuel, which Jacob had named from seeing God face to face, Gill remarks that there was nothing of God in the place now. Clarke supposes they had insultingly pointed to their tower, and Ellicott observes that the citadel which emboldened them to refuse would have been their best shelter from the vengeance they feared.
10:
Where Karkor was, nobody can say. Clarke observes that if it is a place it is nowhere else mentioned, and prefers the derivation which makes the word mean rest, as the Vulgate took it — Zebah and Zalmunna resting with all their army — since the text goes on to say the host was secure. Ellicott keeps it a proper name and glosses it a safe enclosure, reporting that Eusebius and Jerome identified it with a fortress a day's journey from Petra; Gill repeats that identification without deciding, while Ellicott rejects it as too far south to suit the Nobah and Jogbehah of the next verse. Gideon reached it by a roundabout road. Gill has him leave the direct way for the country of the tent-dwellers in order to come on the camp unawares; Ellicott describes the same wide circuit through nomad country, off the main road, as one more attempt to make up by surprise and stratagem for numbers still hopelessly inferior.

The note on Gideon's return has generated a small textual literature. Clarke denies that before the sun was up is a proper translation and would read from the ascent of Chares, with the Greek, Syriac and Arabic behind him. Keil and Delitzsch agree, taking it for a place in front of Succoth of which nothing is known; the Chaldee's before sunset, which the Rabbins and Luther followed, they call flatly contrary to the rules of the language, since the word for ascent cannot be made to mean a setting. Ellicott adds that the preposition simply cannot mean before, and that had the familiar rendering been certain it would have proved a night attack on Karkor; as it stands it suggests rather that Gideon came back by another road. Then the young man is caught. Keil and Delitzsch explain the compressed idiom — Gideon asked him the names of the princes and elders and the boy wrote them down, seventy-seven in all. Ellicott suspects a local council of seventy with their presiding sheykhs, and remarks that the number shows Succoth to have been a place of consequence; Clarke takes them for the men chiefly concerned in the refusal.

The verb that describes the punishment is itself contested. Clarke reports Houbigant's emendation, that instead of he taught we should read he tore, which agrees with the threat and is supported by the Vulgate, Greek, Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic, the two Hebrew letters being easily confused. Ellicott allows the same possibility, that the word may be a misreading for he threshed, and gives Ewald's alternative — that by the elders he taught the rest of the townsmen to be wiser in future. Keil and Delitzsch keep the received text and gloss it: he caused them to know, made them feel, punished them with the thorns. They also defend the justice of it. The two cities had acted treacherously toward Israel from the most selfish interests in a holy conflict, and in despising Gideon and his men had poured contempt on the Lord who had just shown, before the eyes of the whole nation, whose soldiers these were; Gideon, called to be deliverer and judge, was bound to punish them. Ellicott notes that only the elders suffered, Gideon being well aware that in an Oriental city the mass of the people have no voice in such a decision. Gill has the tower beaten down that they had trusted in. Henry draws the general lesson: the active servants of God meet more dangerous opposition from false professors than from open enemies, and must not mind the behaviour of men who are Israelites in name and Midianites in heart; the less help they get and the more hindrance, the more the Lord assists — and many are taught by the briers and thorns of affliction who would learn no other way.
18:
Clarke points out that the question has no antecedent and must be supplied by conjecture: Gideon seems to have had some confused account that his family had been massacred while he was away, and he now puts it to the prisoners, who boldly acknowledge the deed. He may have hoped to exchange the two kings for brothers taken alive, and it is only on learning they were dead that he decrees the death of their murderers — a turn Clarke compares to Aeneas, who stood with his hand held back over the suppliant Turnus until the belt of the slain Pallas caught his eye. Ellicott says the colloquy is plainly given in a shortened form, that the question is really a taunt or an expression of grief, and that we are wholly in the dark about the battle or massacre at Tabor; the brothers may have fallen in Barak's fight there or in some early stage of the Midianite invasion. He notes that they had been kept alive to answer the taunt of Succoth, and may have thought with Agag that the bitterness of death was past. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the word means where, giving instead in what form were the men, and take the reply — every one like the form of kings' sons — for the evidence on which the strict law of retaliation was applied.

Henry reads the exchange as an indictment. His brothers had probably taken shelter in the mountain dens which Israel made for fear of Midian, and were killed there in cold blood; Gideon asks the question not because he is uncertain but so that the murderers' own acknowledgment of the uncommon comeliness of the men should make the crime appear the more heinous. He then observes the choice Gideon made: he might have put them to death as Israel's judge, but he preferred to act as the avenger of blood, next of kin to the slain. Little did they think to hear of it so long after, Henry says, but murder seldom goes unpunished even in this life. Ellicott grounds the same act in the law of retaliation and adds that Jether, as heir, inherited the duties of the avenger, and that Gideon meant at once to train the boy to fearlessness, to give him prestige, and to deepen the disgrace of the kings — though here too, he insists, Gideon is to be judged by the standard of his own day. Gill gives the same reasons and calls it the greater mortification for kings to fall by a youth's hand.

The boy would not draw. Henry notes drily that courage does not always run in the blood. The prisoners then asked to die by Gideon's own hand, which Gill and Ellicott take for a matter of honour and of mercy together — more honourable than dying by a boy, and quicker. Clarke dwells on the shame of falling by a child's blows and their lingering cruelty, and recalls Tacitus on Civilis, who is said to have handed captives to his little son to be shot at with boyish darts — asking whether anything of the kind could have been Gideon's design. The ornaments taken from the camels' necks close the scene. Ellicott identifies them as little moons, crescents of gold and silver still used to decorate animals in the East. Clarke reports that the Greek renders the word crescents, followed by the Syriac and Arabic, and connects it with the ancient worship of the moon among the Ishmaelites, noting that though Mohammed destroyed its idolatrous use the crescent survived on their ensigns and their mosques. Henry takes them for badges either of royalty or of idolatry, Ashteroth being represented by the moon as Baal by the sun, and adds that Gideon did not afterwards put this spoil to so good a use as one would have wished.
22:
Gill has the chief men of Israel meet, consult among themselves and send a deputation with the offer. Henry thinks the offer honest: they judged it reasonable that the man who had borne the toil and peril of their deliverance should hold the honour and power afterwards, and desirable that one who had received such manifest tokens of God's presence should preside over their affairs ever after — and he turns it at once upon Christ, who has delivered us from our worst and most dangerous enemies, and may therefore fitly rule those he has freed to serve him without fear. Ellicott marks the place as the opening of the third great phase of Gideon's life, the phase that holds both his noblest act, the refusal of the kingdom, and his most questionable, the setting up of a schismatic worship. What the people had learned, he says, was the advantage of united action under one great leader; what they forgot was that this leader had a special call from God, and that God was their king.

Clarke is the least patient with them. They were a weak, foolish and inconstant people: their government was a theocracy, and now, dazzled by a man who had been only an instrument in God's hand, they proposed to throw off the divine yoke and shackle themselves with an unlimited hereditary monarchy. He states the political distinction flatly — an unlimited monarchy is a curse, a limited one may be a blessing and even an appointment of God, but the former never can be. Gill draws the line more narrowly: Gideon was not declining the judgeship to which God had raised him, but the kingship, for which he had neither authority nor call, the choice of a king belonging to God and not to the people. Ellicott says the same, that he was willing to be their judge under divine guidance while refusing the splendid temptation of a hereditary crown, and that the day anticipated in the law of the king had not yet come.

Henry finds two things in the refusal. There is modesty in it: what Gideon had done was meant to serve them and not to rule them, and he thought the honour of doing good recompense enough without the honour of bearing sway — nor would he entail grandeur on his family. And there is piety in it. Henry suspects Gideon had discerned in the people a dislike of the theocracy and a hankering after a king like the nations, and that they were using his merits as a colourable pretext for the change; no good man, he concludes, can be pleased with an honour done to himself which belongs peculiarly to God. Clarke observes that few men with such power at command would have answered so, and that the speech calls the nation back to its first principles — he cannot resist contrasting it with Cromwell's reply when the commons offered him the crown of England. Ellicott quotes Cassel's comparison with Washington, who accepted the presidency in order to obey the voice of the people while declaring that no people were more bound to adore the invisible hand which conducts the affairs of men. Up to this point, Ellicott says, we feel all the goodness of Gideon, with something of the past greatness of Joshua in him and something of the future grace of David. Keil and Delitzsch alone see the shadow already. Gideon resisted the crown out of true fidelity, but the appeal carried a second temptation inside it, which he did not resist: to secure for himself in the future the position to which the Lord had called him — the Lord who had appeared to him in His angel, commanded the altar and the atoning sacrifice, and made His will known to him again and again.
24:
Gill notes that the moment was well chosen: men who had just offered him a crown would scarcely deny him a smaller favour. Ellicott turns that into the moral of the whole passage — not seldom the magnanimity which has stood firm under a great trial succumbs to a weaker one, and it would have been better for Gideon's glory had he answered as Abraham did to the king of Sodom. The rings, he notes, served as a kind of currency where there was no coinage. Clarke sees the darker precedent at once: the request is very like Aaron's, when Israel brought their golden earrings and the calf was made of them. Whether Gideon meant his ephod for an instrument of worship or merely for a trophy, Clarke says, is not clear, though it is most likely that he intended to establish a place of worship at Ophrah and took this occasion to provide the vestments for it. Keil and Delitzsch describe the collection, a cloth spread out and every man throwing in the ring he had taken; Ellicott suspects the true reading may be that Gideon himself spread it.

The weight is reckoned at seventeen hundred shekels, and nobody agrees what that comes to. Gill piles up the estimates — one authority making it some eight hundred ounces, another rather more and worth six thousand eight hundred crowns of gold, a third turning it into Hungarian pieces. Clarke takes the shekel at half an ounce and arrives at seventy pounds ten ounces, worth about three thousand one hundred sterling; Ellicott agrees at about seventy pounds and draws the inference, that so many rings imply the slaughter of a great many leading Midianites. Both of them reach for the same parallel, the three bushels of knights' rings emptied on the floor of the Carthaginian senate after Cannae. Keil and Delitzsch are careful to separate what Gideon asked for from what he did not: the fifty pounds of rings stood apart from the crescents, the ear-drops, the purple clothes the kings had worn and the neck-bands of their camels, and all of that the Israelites kept for themselves.

What the ephod was, and what it was for, divides them. Keil and Delitzsch deny flatly that the word means an image of Jehovah or an idol, as Gesenius maintained; it is the shoulder-dress of the high priest, with the breastplate and the Urim and Thummim belonging to it — and they add that the whole fifty pounds need not have gone into the garment, only that the gold paid for it. Ellicott reasons from its splendour: it was by far the most sacred adjunct of worship Israel possessed, and Gideon's object seems to have been a counter-attraction of equally precious materials. He rejects both the reading that makes the ephod an idol and the Rabbinic view that it was merely a memorial of the victory. Gill, weighing the same Jewish opinion, finds it improbable on the plain ground that a garment is a poor monument where a pillar would have served, and concludes that the thing was done with a religious view which was afterwards perverted. Clarke adds the practical objection that no man could wear a coat of nearly a hundred pounds' weight, and guesses that Gideon made a whole tabernacle service in miniature. Ellicott finds the clue in the words about Ophrah: Shiloh lay within the precincts of the fierce tribe that had just quarrelled with him, and Gideon may have been as anxious as Jeroboam later was to keep a direct hold on the nation's worship as one of the secrets of political power. And the word translated snare means not merely a stumbling-block but a cause of ruin. Clarke explains the idiom of going a whoring after it, the nation being reckoned married to God, so that idolatry is a breach of covenant as adultery is of marriage.
28:
Clarke notes that Midian could make head no more during the forty years of Gideon's government. Ellicott treats the verse as closing the second great epoch of Gideon's life, the remaining notices belonging to the third and last. Keil and Delitzsch explain why those notices are given at all: they prepare the way for the history of his sons, in which the sin of Gideon came to a head and the judgment burst upon his house. They find the retirement pointedly told, the phrasing and the sudden name Jerubbaal throwing into relief the change from the heat of war to domestic quiet, as the celebrated Baal-fighter declined the crown and went back into private station. Ellicott thinks the reversion to that name may itself be significant: Baal had failed to plead his own cause, and yet Gideon was not safe from idolatrous tendencies. Gill has him disband the army and retire to Ophrah, though not to live privately, since he continued to act as judge. Henry admires the modesty of it — he was not puffed up by his honours and coveted no palace, but went back to the house he had lived in before his elevation, like the brave Roman who was called from the plough to command an army and returned to his plough when the action was over.

Then the family. Henry notes that Gideon had many wives, and says outright that in this he transgressed the law. Ellicott presses the same point harder: the multitude of wives shows that Gideon was a king in all but name, and this is the most magnificent but the least honourable period of his career, since the law of the king had forbidden precisely this multiplying of wives and of silver and gold. Gill notes that the seventy were not all born after the victory, since Jether was already old enough to be handed a sword. On the concubine the commentators agree in substance and differ in emphasis. Gill and Clarke both define her as a lawful but secondary wife, whose children did not inherit; Gill adds that she was never brought into Gideon's house at all but lived at Shechem, where he met with her when he came to try causes as judge. Ellicott argues from the sequel that she belonged to the Canaanite population of Shechem — in which case Gideon's conduct was as much against the law as Solomon's, though the law was probably far better known in Solomon's reign than in this anarchical period.

The son's name is read as a programme. Clarke takes it to mean my father is king, and holds that the mother gave it, wishing to raise her son to the supreme government and choosing a name that might stimulate him to seek what she hoped he would enjoy in his father's right. Ellicott weighs whether the father set the name on him, having observed the boy's ambitious temper, or the Shechemites and his mother gave it, and prefers the latter; the word carries the force of the dynastic titles of eastern rulers. Abimelech, he says, was a bad reproduction of Gideon, with his father's courage and energy and none of his virtues. Henry, who gives the name the same sense, says simply that he proved the ruin of the family. Gill has him die after forty years, with a large family, wealth and credit; Clarke supplies a date; Keil and Delitzsch mark that he died a peaceful death, which his sons did not, and was buried in his father's grave. Henry's obituary is the warmest — he died in honour and in a good old age, having lived as long as he was capable of serving God and his country. Ellicott's is the coldest: he died in peace and prosperity, but the evil seed he had sown bore bitter fruit in the next generation.
33:
Gill records the relapse in a line: as soon as Gideon was dead they turned from God and the pure worship of him to idolatry. Ellicott quotes the old comment that they returned to their vomit, and finds the moral in the speed of it — the reign of Ahab was to show again how quickly unauthorised symbols degenerate into positive idolatry. After all that had happened, he says, it would have been impossible for a Jerubbaal himself to worship Baal; but his little deflection from the appointed ritual soon became a wide divergence from the national faith. On the name of the new god they divide finely. Keil and Delitzsch insist that Baal-berith does not mean Baal as the god of covenants, but Baal as a god in covenant — a Baal with whom Israel had made a compact, in imitation of the covenant God they already had in Jehovah; the worship at Shechem was accordingly a counterfeit of the worship of Jehovah, with Baal put in his place. Clarke takes the title the other way, as the lord of the covenant, the deity whose business it was to preside over compacts, leagues and treaties, answering to the Jupiter or Mercury of the Romans. Ellicott allows that the Hebrew will bear that sense but thinks the ordinary rendering probably right, and dismisses the attempt to turn Baal-berith into a female deity of Berytus.

Then the forgetting. Gill, following the Targum, makes it the worship of the Lord their God that they forgot, and calls it base ingratitude. Ellicott sees rather the standing tendency to syncretism, the half-way step towards idolatry: they took Baal for their Elohim and forgot that Jehovah was the one God, as Zephaniah's people swore both by the Lord and by Malcham, and the Samaritans feared the Lord and served their own gods. Keil and Delitzsch join the two ingratitudes together, to God and to Gideon, and read the doubled name as deliberate: Jerubbaal-Gideon is written not merely to identify the man but to recall what the Baal-fighter had deserved of Israel. Ellicott, who would also join the two names as the Vulgate does, thinks both of them allusive — he had been the hewer of their enemies and the pleader against Baal, and they repaid him by apostatising to Baal. Clarke objects on plain grammatical grounds to the way the English separates them, since we do not say Simon, namely Peter. Gill supplies the sequel bluntly: what they showed his house was not unkindness merely but cruelty, in the slaughter of his seventy sons.

Clarke closes the chapter with a summing-up of the man. Of Gideon himself the most that can be said is what the angel said, that he was a mighty man of valour. He was a true patriot who hazarded his life for his country, and yet would not stir till he had incontestable proof that God would make him victorious. He was plainly disinterested and void of ambition, refusing a crown that would have altered a constitution acknowledging no ruler but God himself. His motive in making the ephod is not well understood and was probably not reprehensible, but the act was wholly wrong: he had no divine authority for such an innovation in the worship of his country. His private character, Clarke adds, was not very exemplary. Ambrose and Augustine, following Origen, laboured to find a parallel between Gideon and Christ, and Clarke will not go into their details, holding it no credit either to Christ or to Christianity to be compared with such a life. He ends with a rule: where the Spirit of God says a thing is a type, it is our duty to believe and examine; where men produce their own types, it may be our duty to doubt and pass on.
